g12-geography-ug6-t1.overview: Environmental problems such as climate change, ozone depletion, biodiversity loss, pollution and land degradation have become global in their existence and impacts. This lesson examines each major problem and shows that the ecological footprints of poorer nations are vastly lower than those of wealthy nations.
objectives: Describe the major global environmental problems and their worldwide reach
Apply the environment formula I = f(P,A,T) to identify the drivers of global environmental impact
Distinguish primary from secondary air pollutants using named gases
Interpret IUCN and ocean oxygen data to compare the severity of biodiversity loss and ocean exhaustion
Explain land degradation and soil contamination and the GEF programs that respond to them
g12-geography-ug6-t1.simple: Today's environmental problems are global in their causes and their effects. World interest in them grew strongly after the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development in Rio de Janeiro in 1992. Analysts summarize their causes with the environment formula I = f(P,A,T): impacts rise with population growth, affluence or consumption, and environmentally unsound technology. The major global problems are climate change, ozone layer depletion, biodiversity loss, air and water pollution, and land degradation with soil contamination. Wealthy nations and their citizens place far greater demands on the global ecosystem than poorer nations. The ozone layer, found 15 to 30 kilometres above the Earth, shields us from ultraviolet rays, but substances such as CFC destroy it. The IUCN Red List of 2018 records thousands of threatened species, oceans are steadily losing oxygen, and 24 billion tons of fertile soil are lost every year.
g12-geography-ug6-t1.detailed:
A globalized crisis. Environmental problems are now globalized in their existence, their impacts and the socioeconomic factors that generate them. Yet societies contribute unequally: environmental analysts emphasize that the ecological footprints of poorer nations, and of their individual citizens, are vastly lower than those of wealthy nations. Interest in global environmental concerns grew significantly after the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development in Rio de Janeiro in 1992, because even the strongest national environmental policy cannot tackle these challenges alone. The globally interlinked environmental condition is evaluated as a function of population, consumption and technology, expressed in the environment formula I = f(P,A,T), where I is global environmental impact, P is world population growth, A is increasing affluence, that is consumption of goods and services, and T is environmentally unsound technology.

Climate change and ozone depletion. Climatically active greenhouse gases disrupt the Earth's thermal balance by partially blocking thermal radiation into outer space, intensifying the greenhouse effect, and governments have proposed mitigation and adaptation measures for industries and every citizen. The ozone (O3) layer forms a barrier in the stratosphere, about 15 to 30 kilometres above the Earth's surface, protecting humanity from damaging ultraviolet (UV) rays. Ozone-depleting substances such as chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) destroy this layer, letting UV rays reach the surface and cause skin cancer and cataracts. Depletion occurs globally except over tropical areas, and is fastest in the highest latitudes. The Montreal Protocol reduced ozone-depleting substances and protected both the ozone layer and the climate; the replacements, F-gases such as hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs) and sulfur hexafluoride (SF6), are not ozone depleters but are greenhouse gases that are rising in the atmosphere.

Biodiversity loss. Biodiversity embraces all animal and plant species, including microorganisms, the genetic variability within species and the ecosystems in which they live. The United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity was adopted by 154 states at the Rio conference in 1992 and came into effect in December 1993. Despite international agreements, ecosystem degradation and species loss continue rapidly because earlier protection measures do not go far enough and political will and finance are lacking. The IUCN Red List (version 2018-1) shows: of 7,866 described amphibians, 2,100 are threatened; 1,210 of 5,677 mammals; 1,469 of 11,122 birds; 1,236 of 10,711 reptiles; 2,385 of 33,900 fishes; and 12,049 of 268,000 flowering plants.

Air pollution. Air pollution is the intrusion of chemicals, particles or biological elements into the atmosphere that cause discomfort, sickness or death, harm other living creatures, or damage the natural or built environment. Primary pollutants are formed and emitted directly from particular sources: sulfur dioxide (SO2), produced by volcanoes and by burning coal and petroleum, reacts with oxygen to form acid rain; nitrogen dioxide (NO2), expelled by high-temperature combustion and by electric discharge during thunderstorms, appears as the reddish-brown toxic gas of the brown haze dome above cities; carbon monoxide (CO), a colourless, odourless but very poisonous gas from incomplete combustion of charcoal, natural gas, coal, wood and vehicular exhaust, has killed people burning charcoal in confined rooms; volatile organic compounds (VOCs) include methane, an efficient greenhouse gas, and the non-methane compounds benzene, toluene and xylene, suspected of leading to leukemia through prolonged exposure; and particulates are tiny solid or liquid particles suspended in a gas, of which human sources account for about 10 percent of global atmospheric aerosols.

Secondary pollutants, water pollution and ocean exhaustion. Secondary pollutants form in the lower atmosphere by chemical reactions: smog, a word combining smoke and fog, was classically produced by coal burning mixed with sulfur dioxide, while modern photochemical smog forms when vehicular and industrial emissions react under ultraviolet light, and ground-level ozone (O3) forms from nitrogen oxides (NOx) and VOCs. Water pollution occurs when harmful chemicals or microorganisms contaminate a stream, river, lake, ocean, aquifer or other water body; water easily becomes polluted because it dissolves more substances than any other liquid. Pollution from a single source is point source pollution; from diffused sources it is nonpoint source pollution. The marine environment covers roughly 70 percent of the Earth's surface and more than 95 percent of its water. Over the past 50 years the ocean lost about 85 billion tons of oxygen over an area roughly the size of the European Union, the amount of zero-oxygen ocean water quadrupled, and low-oxygen zones, where oxygen has fallen to 2 milligrams per litre or less, increased 10 times; these 'dead zones' persist for thousands of years once established.

Land degradation and soil contamination. Land degradation is a negative trend in land condition caused by human-induced processes, expressed as long-term reduction of biological productivity, ecological integrity or value to humans; it has accompanied humankind since agriculture spread in the Neolithic period, about 10,000 to 7,500 years ago. Degraded land releases soil carbon and nitrous oxide, so it feeds climate change. Scientists warn that 24 billion tons of fertile soil are lost per year, largely through unsustainable agriculture; if the trend continues, 95 percent of the Earth's land could be degraded by 2050, and 3.2 billion people, especially rural communities and poor smallholder farmers, are already affected, while the world population is projected to reach 9.7 billion in 2050. Soil pollution is the presence of harmful substances in amounts that endanger human health or the ecosystem; children are especially susceptible because they play on the ground, and disposed dry cell batteries are a common contaminant. The Global Environmental Facility (GEF) supports three Impact Programs: Food Systems, Land Use and Restoration (FOLUR) for food security through sustainable land management, Sustainable Forest Management (SFM) for drylands, and the Sustainable Cities program, which integrates voluntary Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) targets into urban planning.

keyTerms.def: The demand an individual or nation places on the global ecosystem; those of poorer nations and their citizens are vastly lower than those of wealthy nations.
I = f(P,A,T), where I is global environmental impact, P is world population growth, A is rising affluence or consumption, and T is environmentally unsound technology.
Destruction of the stratospheric ozone (O3) layer, about 15 to 30 kilometres up, by substances such as CFC, allowing harmful UV rays to cause skin cancer and cataracts.
A pollutant formed and emitted directly from a particular source, such as SO2, NO2, CO, VOCs and particulates.
A pollutant formed in the lower atmosphere by chemical reactions, such as smog and ground-level ozone from NOx and VOCs.
A kind of air pollution whose name combines smoke and fog; classic smog came from coal burning, modern photochemical smog from vehicular and industrial emissions acted on by UV light.
A region of the sea where oxygen is severely or entirely depleted and most life cannot survive; their number is increasing as climate change alters ocean chemistry.
A negative trend in land condition, human-induced, shown as long-term loss of biological productivity, ecological integrity or value to humans.

workedExamples.problem: Two countries have similar populations, but the citizens of one consume far more goods and use more unsound technology. Use the environment formula to explain which country creates the greater global environmental impact.
workedExamples.given: I = f(P,A,T); P (population) is similar, but A (affluence or consumption) and T (unsound technology) are much higher in the first country.
workedExamples.formula: I = f(P,A,T)
workedExamples.substitution: Country 1: high P-equivalent, very high A, high T. Country 2: same P, low A, low T.
workedExamples.calculation: Since I rises with A and T as well as P, the wealthy country's impacts multiply even though its population is the same.
workedExamples.answer: The wealthy country creates the greater impact, which explains why the footprints of wealthy nations are vastly larger than those of poorer nations.

workedExamples.problem: Using the IUCN Red List 2018 data, calculate what percentage of described amphibian species are threatened.
workedExamples.given: Described amphibians: 7,866. Threatened amphibians in 2018: 2,100.
workedExamples.formula: Percentage threatened = (threatened species / described species) x 100
workedExamples.answer: About 26.7 percent of described amphibian species were threatened in 2018 - a higher share than mammals or birds, showing amphibians are the most threatened vertebrate group in the table.

workedExamples.problem: Oceanographers measured changes over the past 50 years. Express the growth of zero-oxygen water and of low-oxygen zones as multiples of their former extent, and the lost oxygen as a mass.
workedExamples.given: Over 50 years: about 85 billion tons of oxygen were lost; zero-oxygen ocean water quadrupled; low-oxygen zones increased 10 times over an area about the size of the European Union.
workedExamples.formula: Change factor = new value / old value
workedExamples.substitution: Zero-oxygen: new/old = 4. Low-oxygen zones: new/old = 10.
workedExamples.calculation: 4/1 = 4 times, and 10/1 = 10 times the former extent, with 85 billion tons of oxygen lost overall.
workedExamples.answer: Zero-oxygen water now covers 4 times its former extent and low-oxygen zones 10 times, with 85 billion tons of oxygen lost - evidence of advancing ocean exhaustion.

workedExamples.problem: At the present rate of soil loss, project how much fertile soil the world would lose in a decade, and state the projected share of degraded land by 2050.
workedExamples.given: About 24 billion tons of fertile soil are lost per year; scientists warn 95 percent of the Earth's land areas could be degraded by 2050.
workedExamples.formula: Total loss = annual loss x number of years
workedExamples.substitution: 24 billion x 10 = 240 billion tons.
workedExamples.calculation: 240 billion tons in a decade, against a 2050 projection of 95 percent degraded land and a population of 9.7 billion.
workedExamples.answer: Roughly 240 billion tons of fertile soil in ten years; without rapid remedial action, 95 percent of the Earth's land could be degraded by 2050.

commonMistakes: Believing environmental problems respect borders, when they are globalized in cause and impact.
Assuming poorer nations cause most global damage, although their citizens' footprints are vastly lower than those of wealthy nations.
Confusing the beneficial stratospheric ozone layer with harmful ground-level ozone, a secondary pollutant in smog.
Thinking all pollutants are emitted directly - ground-level ozone and smog form secondarily by chemical reactions in the lower atmosphere.
Believing water pollution always comes from one pipe; nonpoint source pollution comes from diffused sources such as farms and urban areas.
Treating soil contamination as short-lived; once hazardous substances are deposited they cause long-term contamination.
Mixing up the latitudes: ozone depletion is faster at the highest latitudes, not over tropical areas.
applications: Spot local signs of pollution such as the brown haze dome of NO2 above busy city traffic, and never burn charcoal in a closed room after the CO example in the text.
Compare the footprint of a wealthy urban household with that of a rural household in your woreda to explain unequal contributions to global impacts.
Use the IUCN threatened species table to justify why protecting habitats, not only single species, is urgent.
Collect and safely dispose of dry cell batteries instead of dumping them on open ground, the textbook's example of soil contamination.
During a field trip, trace whether a polluting stream receives point or nonpoint source pollution, as Reflective Activity 6.2 asks.
Support Land Degradation Neutrality ideas in your locality, such as terracing slopes, replanting and sustainable farming.
g12-geography-ug6-t1.summary: Environmental problems - climate change, ozone depletion, biodiversity loss, air and water pollution, and land degradation - are globalized in their existence, impacts and causes, and are driven by population, affluence and technology in the formula I = f(P,A,T). The data are stark: thousands of threatened species in the 2018 IUCN Red List, quadrupled zero-oxygen ocean water, and 24 billion tons of fertile soil lost yearly with 3.2 billion people already affected. Wealthy nations carry vastly larger footprints, and responses run from the Montreal Protocol to the GEF's FOLUR, SFM and Sustainable Cities programs.

options: Greenhouse gases intensify by blocking thermal radiation

questions.explanation: F-gases are not ozone-depleting substances but are recognized greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change.

g12-geography-ug6-t2.overview: Continuing current development practices will not achieve sustainable development because challenges such as population growth, urbanization, energy use, water scarcity and waste keep intensifying. This lesson quantifies each challenge and presents proven sustainable solutions, from ocean microbes to solar chimneys and green buildings.
objectives: Explain why continuing current development practices cannot achieve sustainable development
Compute per-person shares of productive land and compare them with actual use to show the limits are exceeded
Describe urbanization trends and list the environmental impacts of urban growth
Evaluate water scarcity and waste management using textbook thresholds and figures
Outline sustainable solutions including climate mitigation with ocean microbes, solar chimneys and green buildings
g12-geography-ug6-t2.simple: Sustainability means making decisions that have no negative consequences for current or future generations. Today's practices fall short because of six rising issues: climate change, hunger, income inequality, rapid urbanization, unmet energy needs and recurring financial crises. The most serious challenges to sustainable development are population growth, urbanization, energy use and global warming, water shortages and waste management. The world had about 7.7 billion people in 2019 and is projected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050. Only one-eighth of the Earth's surface suits human habitation: dividing about 11.2 billion productive hectares among 6.3 billion people gives 1.8 hectares per person, yet we use 2.2, more than 20 percent beyond what is produced annually. Solutions exist and work: oceans and cyanobacteria absorb much human carbon, soil microbes sustain fertility, the solar chimney turns heated air into clean electricity, and green buildings minimize resource use, emissions and waste over their full life cycle.
g12-geography-ug6-t2.detailed:
Why current practices fail. Sustainability means making decisions that do not have negative consequences for either current or future generations, touching everything from preserving natural resources to human wellbeing. The textbook lists six warning signs: climate change impacts may escalate without adequate safeguards; hunger and malnourishment persist in many countries; income inequality within and among countries has reached extremely high levels, invoking the spectre of heightened tension and social conflict; rapid urbanization demands new ways of designing and financing cities; energy needs will remain unmet for hundreds of millions of households without progress in modern energy services; and financial crises must be prevented while redirecting finance toward long-term sustainable investment.

The five great challenges. The sustainability approaches are severely challenged by elements found across the world. The most serious challenges to the planet's sustainable development are population growth, urbanization, energy use and global warming, water shortages, and waste management. Each is measurable, and together they show that the continuation of current development practices will not be enough to achieve sustainable development.

Population growth and the land we actually have. World population was about 7.7 billion in 2019, growing at about 1.1 percent a year; it was only 1.6 billion in 1900 and 3.0 billion in 1960, and the UN projects 8.5 billion in 2030 and 9.7 billion in 2050. Currently about 80 million people are added every year in less developed countries, against only about 1.6 million in more developed countries, so growth is fastest where it cannot be afforded. Productive space is limited: three-quarters of the surface is covered by seas, half of the terrestrial land is desert, and more than a quarter is high mountain, so just one-eighth of the Earth's surface is suitable for human habitation. Dividing the roughly 11.2 billion hectares of productive earth among the 6.3 billion people who depend on it gives about 1.8 hectares per person, yet collectively we use about 2.2 hectares per person - over 20 percent more than is produced annually, meaning the population has already exceeded the sustainable limit.

Urbanization. In 1950 New York was the only city in the world with more than 10 million people; there were 5 such cities in 1975, 17 in 2001 and 21 in 2015. The world's urban population reached 2.9 billion in 2000 and is expected to grow by 2.1 billion by 2030, about 60 percent of humanity. Population growth coupled with urbanization brings significant environmental impacts: increased ambient temperature, decreased air quality, increased water run-off, decreased quality of run-off water, altered weather patterns, loss of natural beauty, reduction in farmlands and subsequent food shortage, and deforestation.

Energy use and global warming. There is a broad relation between wealth and energy consumption. India's energy consumption rose threefold, from 4.16 to 12.8 quadrillion Btu, between 1980 and 2001. The US Department of Energy's international outlook projects that China and India will account for nearly one-half of the total increase in residential energy use in non-OECD countries by 2030, and the OECD brings together 38 member countries. Although the greenhouse effect occurs naturally, human activity is increasing the atmospheric concentrations of the responsible gases: over one-third of human-induced greenhouse gases come from burning fossil fuels to generate electricity, and all fossil fuels release carbon dioxide when burned.

Water scarcity and waste. According to the UN, one out of every six people lacks access to safe drinking water, and more than double that number lack adequate sanitation. Only about 2.5 percent of the Earth's water is fresh, and three-quarters of that is locked in glaciers and permanent snow; only 0.3 percent is the easily accessible surface water of rivers and lakes. Ground and surface water are being used faster than they are replenished, and a country is considered water-scarce when its annual supply of renewable freshwater is less than 1,000 cubic metres per capita. On waste: the world generates 2.01 billion tons of municipal solid garbage a year, at least 33 percent of it not managed in an ecologically sound manner; the average person generates 0.75 kilograms a day, ranging from 0.11 to 4.54 kilograms. High-income nations, only 16 percent of world population, produce 34 percent - 683 million tons - of global garbage, and global waste is predicted to rise to 3.4 billion tons by 2050. Waste management methods include disposal (landfill and incineration), recycling (physical and biological processing), energy recovery, and avoidance and reduction.

Sustainable solutions. True solutions go beyond technical fixes. To combat climate change, note that oceans are the largest carbon reservoir on Earth and consume about one-third of all human carbon emissions; about half of the Earth's carbon dioxide is fixed by cyanobacteria and other ocean microbes through photosynthesis, and the carbon-rich lipids they produce can be used for biofuel. Preserving ecologically significant regions, developing friendly energy and waste systems, and using biofuels also mitigate warming. In sustainable agriculture, soil microorganisms maintain the fertility of agro-ecosystems, but heavy chemical inputs are depleting them, so introducing beneficial microbes raises yields acceptably. In renewable energy, the solar chimney - consisting of a glass roof collector, a chimney and a wind turbine - heats air under a huge greenhouse-like circular roof; convection makes the air rise and escape through the tall tower, driving turbines that produce electricity with enormous energy yield, no ecological breakdown, minimal cost and no safety hazards, unlike nuclear plants, and no depletion of natural resources. Finally, green buildings achieve high performance over the full life cycle by minimizing natural resource consumption, minimizing harmful indoor and outdoor emissions, minimizing solid and liquid waste discharge, and keeping negative impact on the site ecosystem low.

keyTerms.def: Making decisions that do not have negative consequences for either current or future generations, spanning natural resources and human wellbeing.
The limited land and sea area able to supply human needs - only one-eighth of the Earth's surface is believed suitable for human habitation.
The growth of cities and city populations; the world's urban population reached 2.9 billion in 2000 and is projected to be about 60 percent of humanity by 2030.
A condition in which a country's annual supply of renewable freshwater is less than 1,000 cubic metres per capita.
The collection, transport, processing, recycling or disposal of waste materials to protect health, the environment and resources.
One of the waste management methods, alongside disposal (landfill and incineration), recycling, and avoidance and reduction.
A renewable power plant of three elements - glass roof collector, chimney and wind turbine - in which heated air rises by convection and drives turbines.
A building that performs highly over its full life cycle by minimizing resource consumption, emissions, waste discharge and impact on the site ecosystem.

workedExamples.problem: Using the textbook's figures, calculate the average productive land available per person and compare it with what is actually used. What does the result mean for sustainability?
workedExamples.given: About 11.2 billion hectares of productive earth; 6.3 billion people depending on it; actual collective use about 2.2 hectares per person.
workedExamples.formula: Available per person = productive hectares / population; Overuse = use - available
workedExamples.substitution: 11.2 billion / 6.3 billion = 1.78; 2.2 - 1.8 = 0.4 hectares per person.
workedExamples.calculation: 1.78 rounds to about 1.8 hectares per person available, but 2.2 hectares are used - roughly 20 percent more than the Earth produces annually.
workedExamples.answer: About 1.8 hectares per person are available while 2.2 are used, so humanity has already exceeded the sustainable limit.

workedExamples.problem: Track the growth of megacities with more than 10 million people, then state the expected share of the world population living in cities by 2030.
workedExamples.given: 1950: only New York qualified; 1975: 5 cities; 2001: 17 cities; 2015: 21 cities; urban population 2.9 billion in 2000.
workedExamples.formula: Growth = number of later cities - number of earlier cities
workedExamples.calculation: The count quadrupled between 2001 and 2015, and the urban population is expected to increase by 2.1 billion by 2030.
workedExamples.answer: By 2015 there were 21 megacities (4 more than in 2001), and urban dwellers will make up roughly 60 percent of the world's population by 2030.

workedExamples.problem: A country's annual renewable freshwater supply is 800 cubic metres per capita. Is it water-scarce, and what global statistics confirm the urgency of the problem?
workedExamples.given: Annual renewable freshwater: 800 m3 per capita; textbook threshold: less than 1,000 m3 per capita marks water scarcity.
workedExamples.formula: Compare supply with the threshold: 800 m3 < 1,000 m3
workedExamples.substitution: 800 is below the 1,000 cubic metre threshold.
workedExamples.calculation: The country is water-scarce. Globally, only 2.5 percent of water is fresh, three-quarters of that is locked in glaciers and snow, only 0.3 percent is accessible surface water, and one in six people lacks safe drinking water.
workedExamples.answer: Yes - with 800 cubic metres per capita the country is water-scarce, reflecting a global crisis in which fresh, accessible water is extremely limited.

workedExamples.problem: Global municipal solid waste is 2.01 billion tons a year and is projected to reach 3.4 billion tons by 2050. Calculate the percentage increase, and state how much waste high-income nations generate.
workedExamples.given: Current waste: 2.01 billion tons; projected 3.4 billion tons by 2050; high-income nations produce 34 percent (683 million tons) with 16 percent of population.
workedExamples.formula: Percentage increase = ((projected - current) / current) x 100
workedExamples.calculation: 1.39 / 2.01 = 0.69, so about 69 percent. High-income nations produce 683 million tons annually.
workedExamples.answer: Waste is projected to rise by about 69 percent to 3.4 billion tons by 2050; high-income nations already generate 34 percent of the world's garbage despite having 16 percent of its population.

commonMistakes: Confusing sustainability with stopping development, when it means decisions without negative consequences for current or future generations.
Assuming the world still has spare productive capacity, when we already use over 20 percent more than the Earth produces annually.
Believing population grows equally everywhere - 80 million are added yearly in less developed countries versus 1.6 million in more developed ones.
Thinking water scarcity depends only on rainfall; the 1,000 cubic metres per capita threshold and the tiny share of accessible surface water matter.
Reducing waste management to open dumping instead of the four method groups: disposal, recycling, energy recovery, avoidance and reduction.
Assuming solar chimneys carry nuclear-style safety hazards or heavy resource depletion - the textbook lists these as advantages that are absent.
Judging a building green only by its looks, when green design is defined by performance over the full life cycle in four areas.
applications: Relate the fast growth of Ethiopian cities to the textbook's urban impacts: higher ambient temperature, poorer air quality, more run-off, lost farmland and deforestation.
Use the 1.8 versus 2.2 hectare figures to explain to your community why consumption restraint and land productivity matter.
Promote household water saving after noting that only 0.3 percent of the Earth's water is easily accessible surface water.
Separate household waste for composting and recycling instead of open dumping, drawing on the four waste management methods.
Discuss how high solar radiation, like that over deserts, could support solar chimney-style renewable projects in Ethiopia's dry areas.
Audit your school building for energy, water and waste performance and propose green building improvements over its life cycle.
g12-geography-ug6-t2.summary: Sustainability requires decisions without negative consequences for present and future generations, yet the challenges of population growth (7.7 billion in 2019, 9.7 billion projected for 2050), urbanization (21 megacities by 2015, about 60 percent urban by 2030), energy use, water scarcity (below 1,000 cubic metres per capita) and waste (2.01 billion tons yearly) remain hard. Humanity already uses 2.2 hectares per person against 1.8 available, exceeding the sustainable limit. Tested solutions include ocean microbes that fix carbon, soil microbes for sustainable agriculture, solar chimneys for clean power and green buildings designed for full life cycle performance.

config.title: How a Solar Chimney Generates Power

steps.label: Collect
steps.detail: The glass roof collector traps solar energy over a huge circular area, like a greenhouse.

steps.label: Heat
steps.detail: Air inside is heated strongly under the roof.

steps.label: Rise
steps.detail: Convection makes the hot air rise up the tall central tower.

steps.label: Drive
steps.detail: The escaping moving air spins the wind turbine at the base.

steps.label: Deliver
steps.detail: Electricity is produced with no ecological breakdown and no resource depletion.

g12-geography-ug6-t3.overview: Environmental education develops an ecologically literate population that is confident and motivated to act on issues from climate change to water shortages. This lesson explains its essence, its formal, informal and tacit forms, and the characteristics that make it lifelong, interdisciplinary and a proven strategy.
objectives: Explain the essence and the three founding goals of environmental education
Differentiate formal, informal and tacit forms of environmental learning with named settings
Arrange the continuum of strategies from information activities to capacity building
Describe the fundamental characteristics of environmental education
Trace the historical roots of environmental education from Rousseau to conservation education
g12-geography-ug6-t3.simple: Environmental education is education in, about, and for the environment. Its primary goal is to develop an ecologically educated population that is confident and motivated to act on critical issues from climate change and habitat protection to endangered species and water shortages. It engages students, community members, policy makers, the young and the old, and it happens in settings from schools and museums to courthouses and boardrooms. Learning may be formal, in traditional schools; informal, in broader public settings such as zoos, aquariums and documentaries; or tacit, gained by living alongside and imitating others. Its strategies form a continuum: information, communication, education and capacity building activities. Environmental education is lifelong, interdisciplinary, hands-on and contextualized, teaches people how to think rather than what to think, and builds on a theory of change. Its origins go back to the 18th century, when Rousseau called for environment-focused education.
g12-geography-ug6-t3.detailed:
The primary goals. Environmental education seeks to develop an ecologically educated population that is self-assured and motivated to take action on critical environmental challenges, from climate change to habitat protection, and from endangered species to water shortages. It is about engaging students, community members and policy makers, the young and the old; it is about empowerment, skills development and providing opportunities for action. It is a strategy by which people make proactive, informed decisions that honour ecological, economic and social integrity as the foundations of sustainability.

Its essence: in, about and for the environment. Most simply, environmental education is education in, about, and for the environment. Researchers have described it broadly as an approach, a philosophy, a tool and a profession, and it is built on three goals: first, to foster clear awareness of and concern about economic, social, political and ecological interdependence in urban and rural areas; second, to provide every person with opportunities to acquire the knowledge, values, attitudes, commitment and skills needed to protect and improve the environment; and third, to create new patterns of behaviour of individuals, groups and society as a whole toward the environment.

Audiences, settings and forms. Its audiences range from youth to the elderly, and from families to policy makers; its settings range from schools and courthouses to museums and boardrooms. Formal environmental education occurs in traditional school settings. Informal (non-formal) education happens in broader public settings such as zoos, aquariums or community centres, and through media outlets such as the Internet or television documentaries. Tacit knowledge is learning from the actions of others - information we obtain implicitly by living together, through contacts or by socializing, without any teaching.

The strategy continuum. Environmental education uses a range of strategies that can be used separately but are ideally built one upon the other. Information activities aim to increase awareness and understanding and count as informal education. Communication activities, in both formal and informal settings, establish a dialogue between audiences and environmental organizations or agencies for mutual sharing of experiences, priorities and planning. Education activities, also in both settings, promote knowledge, understanding, an attitude of concern, and the motivation and capacity to work with others. Capacity building activities, delivered mainly in informal settings, increase the capacity of civil society to support and work for environmental preservation. In practice it is hands-on, contextualized and interdisciplinary, linking natural and social sciences, the arts and mathematics.

Lifelong and interdisciplinary. Environmental education is a lifelong strategy involving everyone - not only the youth, who are a critical audience, but also the adults whose daily consumer behaviours and political actions strongly affect conservation. It involves employees, policy makers, clergy, community activists, parents, grandparents and members of the media, and it reaches people through schools, zoos, aquariums, museums, community centres, parks and media including the Internet, radio, magazines and newspapers. It is interdisciplinary by definition: geography, ecology, biology, chemistry and physics provide vital foundations, but social studies, government studies and history are just as important, because it is social in nature - it is about human behaviour and human interactions with the world.

A proven strategy: how and where it began. Policy tools of regulation and market incentives are often insufficient for environmental management, so managers turn to education, information and voluntary measures. Education does not automatically equal behaviour change, but a strong link is often found, so supporting environmental education is an investment in the future. Well-designed initiatives rest on a theory of change - the idea that a logical series of events demonstrates how activities in the present lead to future goals - and can shape attitudes, knowledge and skills longer than one law or one planted acre. Good environmental education teaches people how to think, not what to think, building citizen-action skills and opportunities to use them. Historically, its origins reach back to the 18th century, when Jean-Jacques Rousseau emphasized the necessity of an environment-focused education; after the Great Depression and the Dust Bowl of the 1920s and 1930s, conservation education emerged as a new kind of environmental education.

commonMistakes: Thinking environmental education is only for children and schools, when it is lifelong and reaches employees, policy makers, clergy and the media.
Treating it as a purely natural-science subject, when it is social in nature and interdisciplinary, including history and government studies.
Assuming more education always equals instant behaviour change; the link is strong but not automatic.
Calling a zoo visit or TV documentary formal education; those are informal settings, while formal means traditional schooling.
Believing environmental education tells people what to think; it teaches people how to think, avoiding advocacy of specific positions.
Counting a one-off poster as the whole strategy; the continuum - information, communication, education, capacity building - should build one upon the other.
Believing it began in modern times; its origins trace to the 18th century with Rousseau and to conservation education after the Dust Bowl.
applications: Join or revive your school's environmental protection club and plan awareness events for the community.

Learn tacitly from elders and practising farmers - observing, living together and imitating their conservation habits.
Train community members (capacity building) so a local project survives without outside help.
Design a hands-on, interdisciplinary school project linking geography, chemistry and art around cleaning a local river.
Teach peers how to think through an environmental dilemma rather than handing them a pre-made position.
g12-geography-ug6-t3.summary: Environmental education is education in, about and for the environment, with three goals: awareness of social and ecological interdependence, acquisition of knowledge, values and skills, and new patterns of behaviour. It reaches every age in formal, informal and tacit forms, and works through a continuum of information, communication, education and capacity building activities. Because it is lifelong, interdisciplinary and grounded in a theory of change - teaching people how to think, not what to think - it is a proven long-term strategy, with roots in Rousseau and in the conservation education born of the 1930s Dust Bowl.

g12-geography-ug6-t4.overview: An environmental movement is a type of social movement in which individuals, groups and coalitions act together to change environmental policies and practices. This lesson classifies the main movement types, from free market environmentalism to Light, Dark and Bright Greens, and reviews Ethiopian initiatives such as LEM Ethiopia and the Green Legacy.
objectives: Define an environmental movement and describe how diverse its forms and spatial scopes are
Classify free market environmentalism, preservation and conservation, and popular environmentalism
Differentiate Light, Dark and Bright Green approaches to environmental change
Describe the state and history of environmental movements in Ethiopia
Evaluate Ethiopian initiatives such as LEM Ethiopia, the waste campaign of Sileshi Demise and the Green Legacy
g12-geography-ug6-t4.simple: An environmental movement is a social movement made up of individuals, groups and coalitions who share an interest in environmental protection and act to change environmental policies and practices. Its forms range from highly organized institutions to radically informal networks, its scope from the local to the almost global. The types include free market environmentalism, which trusts property rights and tort law; preservation, which strictly sets nature aside, versus conservation, which allows sustainable use; and popular environmentalism, whose sustainable consumer habits draw criticism as elitist. Activists are also described as Light Greens, focusing on lifestyle; Dark Greens, seeking radical political change; and Bright Greens, relying on better designs, new technologies and innovations. In Ethiopia, movements are rarely well organized, but LEM Ethiopia, founded in 1992 by 29 professionals, the artist Sileshi Demise, the climate leadership of Meles Zenawi and the Green Legacy campaign of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed show what individuals and organizations can do.
g12-geography-ug6-t4.detailed:
The concept. An environmental movement is a type of social movement involving an array of individuals, groups and coalitions that perceive a common interest in environmental protection and act to bring about changes in environmental policies and practices. Movements are conceived as broad networks of people and organizations engaged in collective action in pursuit of environmental benefits. They are very diverse and complex: their organizational forms range from the highly organized and formally institutionalized to the radically informal; their spatial scope ranges from the local to the almost global; and their concerns range from single issues to the full panoply of global environmental concerns. A movement may be initiated by any group or individuals from anywhere - for example Greta Thunberg, a significant young climate change campaigner whose voice can influence governmental and non-governmental decision-making bodies worldwide.

Free market environmentalism; preservation and conservation. Free market environmentalism contends that the free market, property rights and tort law are the greatest tools for preserving the health and sustainability of the environment - in sharp contrast to the prevalent strategy of relying on legislative government action. Environmental care is regarded as natural, as is the expulsion of polluters and other aggressors by individual and class action. Preservation is the strict setting aside of natural resources to prevent damage caused by human contact or activities such as logging, mining, hunting and fishing. Conservation differs in that it allows some degree of industrial growth while keeping it within sustainable bounds, and regulations and laws may be enacted for it; elsewhere in the world the two are often used interchangeably.

Popular environmentalism. Environmentalist action has recently produced a new subculture, composed mainly of the educated middle and upper class, that practises sustainable consumption - choosing local and organic products over conventionally imported ones manufactured using pesticides and preservatives. Critics call this 'green consumerism' a form of elitism, mere shopping under the banner of environmentalism, and suggest it diverts attention from the fundamental issues serious environmentalists want to tackle; because organic items are often more expensive, buying them can look like a sign of affluence. Others reply that green consumers are not only saving money, and that the cost of environmentally friendly products should simply be reduced.

Light, Dark and Bright Greens. Contemporary environmentalists are often split into three groups. Light Greens see protecting the environment first and foremost as a personal responsibility; they are reformist, do not seek fundamental political reform, and treat environmentalism as a lifestyle choice - expressed in the motto 'Green is the new black'. Dark Greens believe environmental problems are an inherent part of industrialized capitalism and seek radical political change; they hold that prevailing ideas, industrialism, are corrupt and lead to consumerism, alienation from nature and resource depletion, driven by the emphasis on growth that exists in all existing ideologies - a tendency they call 'growth mania'. Bright Greens, the most recent group, believe radical changes are needed to make society sustainable but that better designs, new technologies and widely distributed social innovations are the means; we can neither shop nor protest our way to sustainability, so they focus less on the problems than on the tools, models and ideas that already exist.

Environmental movements in Ethiopia. Environmental activism is rarely seen in Ethiopia in a well-organized way, though initiatives have tried to mainstream environmental problems through governmental ministries, religious and civic organizations. One organization devoted specifically to the environment is LEM Ethiopia, the Environment and Development Society of Ethiopia, founded in 1992 by 29 prominent Ethiopian professionals in environment and development. It promotes sustainable development through natural resource management and appropriate technology promotion, urban waste management and livelihood security, working with donors, government institutions, local and international NGOs and communities, and through capacity building - especially environmental education targeting school children, teachers, farmers, urban dwellers, men, women and development practitioners - while advocating environmental protection policies and climate action.

Individual actions and the way forward. Individual attempts in Ethiopia have been ad hoc and discontinuous but influential. The artist Sileshi Demise (Gash Abera Molla) led a municipal solid waste controlling task with great impact on the Addis Ababa community, and it can be seen as a precursor of the current riparian buffer projects of Addis Ababa. The late Prime Minister Meles Zenawi was officially assigned by African countries to represent the Continent in global climate change negotiations, and Ethiopia is leading the 'green economy' movement in Africa in both ideological and practical terms. The current Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed launched the Green Legacy, with over four billion seedlings claimed to be planted in the first campaign in 2019 during the rainy season, raised to five billion seedlings in 2020, alongside big ecotourism projects across the country. Yet Ethiopian youth, though increasingly affected by environmental and climate issues, are largely absent from policy arenas - a pressing moral need, since they will inherit the environment adults create today, and a political need as well, because such voices inform and contribute to global activism that forces influential political decisions.

commonMistakes: Assuming environmental movements exist only in wealthy countries; Ethiopian examples such as LEM Ethiopia and the Green Legacy exist too.
Concluding Ethiopia has no environmental activity at all; attempts exist but are rarely well organized, ad hoc and discontinuous.
Confusing preservation with conservation - preservation sets nature strictly aside, while conservation allows sustainable industrial growth.
Believing Bright Greens mainly protest; they focus on tools, models and ideas, better designs and new technologies, since we can neither shop nor protest our way to sustainability.
Assuming Light Greens seek radical political reform; they are reformist lifestyle environmentalists.
Thinking only large organizations can start a movement, though it may be initiated by any individual from anywhere, like Greta Thunberg.
Believing green consumerism automatically equals deep environmentalism; critics call it elitist shopping that distracts from fundamental issues.
applications: Join or found a school environmental club and treat it as a mini-movement with policies and practices you can actually change.

Model your actions on individual movers such as Sileshi Demise (Gash Abera Molla), whose waste campaign transformed Addis Ababa habits.
Where affordable, prefer local and organic products, while discussing fairly the elitism criticism raised against green consumerism.
Bring youth voices into local environmental and climate debates, since young people's perspectives are largely absent from policy arenas.
g12-geography-ug6-t4.summary: Environmental movements are broad, diverse social networks acting to change environmental policies and practices, from free market environmentalism and preservation versus conservation, through popular environmentalism, to Light, Dark and Bright Green streams. Ethiopia's activism is rarely well organized, yet LEM Ethiopia (founded 1992 by 29 professionals), the waste campaign of Sileshi Demise, Meles Zenawi's climate leadership for Africa and Abiy Ahmed's Green Legacy - over 4 billion seedlings in 2019, 5 billion in 2020 - show organized and individual power. Youth voices still need a place in Ethiopia's environmental policy arenas.

g12-geography-ug6-t5.overview: Indigenous knowledge is unique, traditional, local, community-based knowledge developed through trial and error in a specific geographic area. This lesson surveys Ethiopia's environmentally friendly practices, from Maccaa Oromo folk medicine and Konso terracing to Gedeo sacred tree respect and Gumuz belief systems and shifting cultivation.
objectives: Define indigenous knowledge and list its characteristic qualities
Identify the areas of resource management where indigenous knowledge is applied
Describe folk medicinal protection practices of the Illuababora Maccaa Oromo in the wet western highlands
Explain Konso dry stone terracing and the Gedeo seera and songo tree prohibitions
Assess the Gumuz belief system of Yamba and Missa and their shifting cultivation for sustainability
g12-geography-ug6-t5.simple: Indigenous knowledge is the unique, traditional, local knowledge of people native to a particular geographic area. It is holistic, dynamic and community-based, built by trial and error through social practice. It is local and rooted in place, transmitted orally or by imitation, strengthened by everyday experience and repetition, widely shared as 'people's science', and organized basically around practical functions. It is applied in ecosystem and landscape management, water management, soil conservation, biological control of pests, ecological agriculture and livestock practices, and plant and animal breeding, all of which enhance food security and fight poverty. Ethiopia, with over 80 ethnic groups, offers rich examples: the Illuababora Maccaa Oromo protect folk medicinal plants in habitats, gardens and sacred groves; the Konso built dry stone terraces up to 5 metres high and hilltop walled towns called Paleta; the Gedeo guard songo sacred trees under seera rules; and the Gumuz hold resources as sacred gifts of Yamba, held in trust by the whole community.
g12-geography-ug6-t5.detailed:
What indigenous knowledge is. Indigenous knowledge is the unique, traditional, local knowledge existing within and developed around the specific conditions of women and men indigenous to a particular geographic area. It is holistic, dynamic and changing, community-based, and generated through trial and error by social practice. Its defining qualities: it is local, rooted in a particular place and set of experiences; orally transmitted, or passed on through imitation and demonstration; a product of practical engagement in everyday life, constantly reinforced by experience; marked by repetition, since repetition is the essential characteristic of tradition; a fluid and transforming agent whose central concept, when applied to knowledge, is negotiation; shared to a much greater degree than other knowledge, so it is frequently called 'people's science'; always somewhat fragmentary in distribution even when it coheres in rituals; essentially functional in organization where it is densest and most applicable; and situated within broader cultural traditions, so separating the technical from the non-technical is problematic.

Where it works - and the western wet highlands. Indigenous knowledge is applied in ecosystem and landscape management, water management, soil conservation, biological control of pests and diseases, ecological agriculture and livestock practices, and plant and animal breeding, which often enhance food security and prevent or alleviate poverty. Ethiopia has over 80 ethnic groups and a rich diversity of such knowledge. In the wet highland landscape of the west, among the Illuababora Maccaa Oromo, indigenous knowledge promotes and preserves the ecosystem. Their folk healing practices protect the health of livestock and families: folk healers and local elders identify and classify medicines and their resources, prepare them, control doses, and keep spiritual and philosophical understandings of folk medicine. They protect folk medicinal plants and other remedy sources from extinction, conserving them in natural habitats, in farmland, pilgrimage and ritual sites, sacred groves, around rivers and in home gardens - even planting medicinal plants secretly in gardens. Culturally, intentionally cutting trees and killing animals is seen as breaking the norms and values of the society, and people believe they keep access to medicines only as long as they protect their environment.

Paractising the dry southern highlands: Konso terracing. The Konso Cultural Landscape, in the dry highland landscape of the south, is characterized by extensive dry stone terraces that witness hundreds of years of persistent human struggle to harness a hard, dry and rocky environment. The terraces retain soil from erosion, collect the maximum water and discharge the excess, and create terrace saddles used for agriculture; the hills are contoured by dry stone terraces that reach up to 5 metres high in places. The dry stone walled towns, called Paleta, stand on high hills chosen for strategic and defensive advantage, circled by between one and six rounds of dry stone defensive walls built from locally available rock.

Gedeo seera and sacred trees. Among the Gedeo people, life rests on long-standing regulations (seera) of standards, respect for elders and oral declarations handed down through generations. Crucially, the value of respect is directed at all species, including domestic animals and the surrounding ecosystem. Respect is shown in reverence for particular environmental resources: songo sacred trees (Dhadacha) are ritualistic trees maintained and protected by prohibition systems (taboos) and traditional seera rules. Disrespectful and prohibited deeds include cutting songo sacred trees, injuring sacred forests, felling young and immature plants from farms, cutting grave trees for house use, defecating in sacred natural sites, and mass-cutting of trees from the indigenous cultural agroforestry landscape - each treated as perjury of ancestral seera.

Gumuz beliefs and shifting cultivation. In the western lowland dry lands, the Gumuz have a special relationship with their lands, knowing their resources through observation and experience and within their traditional belief system. They hold that vital natural and land resources are sacred - the ingenuous gift, blessing and creation of Yamba, the supreme deity and source of life and livelihoods to past, present and future generations; Yamba gave them knowledge of proper use and management and the responsibility to pass resources on. Each resource has its respective Missa (poly-spirits) that ensure proper use and management, and violations bring severe punishment and revenge from the respective Missa. Natural resources are perceived as an ancestral heritage: ownership is vested in the whole community, the present generation holds a trusteeship, and since resources do not belong to one generation alone they cannot be privately possessed or controlled by any single member - only their fruits may be taken. Shifting cultivation, an indigenous agro-ecological practice, maintains the complex agro-ecosystem: fields shift to use the nutrients of the natural vegetation-soil complex, and by skilfully maintaining the natural forest and vegetation ecosystem, soil, water and wild animals are managed sustainably.

Why these practices matter. Environmental degradation needs to be combated by interdisciplinary, multidimensional approaches, one of which is the indigenous knowledge system. Because it is highly influenced by location rather than being a universal concept, indigenous knowledge is used in natural resource management as a supplement to scientific methods of ecological management, or as a substitute for baseline environmental data where little recorded scientific data exists - a reason to identify, document and support the proven practices of one's own community.

keyTerms.def: The unique, traditional, local knowledge existing within and developed around the specific conditions of people indigenous to a particular geographic area; holistic, dynamic and community-based.
Community and folk-healer knowledge of identifying, classifying, preparing and dosing traditional medicines, and of protecting their plant and animal sources.
Building steps of wall on slopes - such as the Konso dry stone terraces reaching up to 5 metres - to retain soil, collect water and create farmable saddles.
The dry stone walled towns of the Konso, set on high hills for strategic and defensive advantage and circled by one to six rounds of dry stone defensive walls.
The long-standing Gedeo regulations of standards, respect to elders and oral declarations passed down generations, protecting songo trees by taboos.
The Gedeo sacred ritualistic trees, maintained and protected by prohibiton systems (taboos) and traditional seera rules.
The supreme deity of the Gumuz, source of life to past, present and future generations; every resource has its Missa (poly-spirits) that punish violations.
The Gumuz practice of shifting fields to use the nutrients of the natural vegetation-soil complex, sustaining forests, soil, water and wildlife.

workedExamples.problem: Match each Ethiopian people to its landscape and practice: Konso, Gedeo, Gumuz, Illuababora Maccaa Oromo - with dry stone terracing and Paleta towns, seera and songo sacred trees with agroforestry, Yamba and Missa beliefs with shifting cultivation, and folk medicine protection with sacred groves.
workedExamples.given: L landscapes: wet highlands of the west; dry highlands of the south; western lowland dry lands; the Gedeo cultural landscape.
workedExamples.formula: Place each practice in its named landscape.
workedExamples.substitution: Konso - southern dry highlands; Illuababora Maccaa Oromo - wet western highlands; Gumuz - western lowlands; Gedeo - agroforestry landscape with sang sacred trees.
workedExamples.calculation: Each people's signature practice belongs to its textbook landscape.
workedExamples.answer: Konso = dry southern highlands (terraces, Paleta); Gedeo = seera and songo trees in agroforestry; Gumuz = western lowlands (Yamba, Missa, shifting cultivation); Illuababora Maccaa Oromo = wet western highlands (folk medicine).

workedExamples.problem: Interpret the engineering facts of the Konso Cultural Landscape: terraces up to 5 metres high, towns circled by one to six rounds of walls, and terrace saddles used for agriculture. What does each feature achieve for soil and water?
workedExamples.given: Terraces retain soil from erosion, collect maximum water and discharge the excess; saddles are used for agriculture.
workedExamples.formula: Link each observed feature to its stated function.
workedExamples.substitution: High terraces = strong soil retention and water storage; multiple wall rounds = town defence; saddles = flat farming surfaces.
workedExamples.calculation: Feature-function pairing shows hundreds of years of adapting to a hard, dry and rocky environment.
workedExamples.answer: The terraces stop erosion and store water while draining excess, the wall rounds protect the hilltop Paleta, and the saddles turn the walls into farmland.

workedExamples.problem: A Gumuz household wants to use its forest's fruit and honey. Apply the community's ownership rules to decide what it may and may not do.
workedExamples.given: Ownership of natural resources is vested in the whole community; the present generation holds trusteeship; resources cannot be privately possessed - only their fruits.
workedExamples.formula: Test the action against communal ownership and trusteeship.
workedExamples.substitution: Taking fruits = allowed; claiming private ownership of the land or forest itself = not allowed.
workedExamples.calculation: Because resources are an ancestral heritage for past, present and future generations, no single member may control them, and each resource's Missa punishes violations.
workedExamples.answer: The household may take the fruits in proper ways, but may not privatize or hoard the resource itself, which belongs to the community across generations.

workedExamples.problem: Decide which of these acts violate Gedeo seera: harvesting mature crops; cutting a songo sacred tree; felling young immature plants from a farm; pruning a home-garden shrub; mass-cutting trees from the agroforestry landscape.
workedExamples.given: Prohibited deeds include cutting songo trees, felling young immature plants, cutting grave trees, defacing sacred sites and mass-cutting of trees.
workedExamples.formula: Compare each act with the list of disrespectful deeds.
workedExamples.substitution: Normal farm work of mature plants is not listed; the three taboos are explicitly named.
workedExamples.calculation: The first and last ordinary acts stay outside the taboo list; the listed deeds break ancestral seera.
workedExamples.answer: Cutting the songo tree, felling immature plants and mass-cutting violate seera; ordinary harvesting and pruning of non-taboo plants do not.

commonMistakes: Treating indigenous knowledge as a universal concept, when it is highly influenced by location and varies across societies.
Assuming it is written down in books; it is orally transmitted, or passed on through imitation and demonstration.
Assuming scientific and indigenous knowledge are rivals; indigenous knowledge supplements scientific methods and substitutes baseline data where records are scarce.
Believing Gumuz resources belong to private owners; ownership is vested in the whole community, which holds trusteeship - only fruits may be taken.

Mixing up localities: Konso terracing is in the dry southern highlands, Gedeo agroforestry with songo trees is a separate cultural landscape, and Maccaa Oromo folk medicine belongs to the wet western highlands.
Thinking the Gedeo ban all cutting in every context; the prohibitions target songo sacred trees, grave trees, young immature plants, sacred sites and mass-cutting.
Calling indigenous knowledge static; it is dynamic and changing, with tradition as a fluid and transforming agent whose central concept is negotiation.
applications: Identify and document the most prevalent indigenous conservation practices in your own area and present them in class as the textbook's activity asks.
Study the Konso terraces as a model when designing soil and water conservation works on eroding slopes in your region.
Learn from folk healers and elders how medicinal plants are protected in farmplots, ritual sites and home gardens, and copy the practice locally.
Respect sacred groves and trees and support the taboos and traditional rules that keep them standing.
Apply the Gumuz lesson of trusteeship by sharing communal resources - pastures, springs, forests - fairly rather than privatizing them.
Use indigenous knowledge of biological pest control and ecological agriculture to raise yields without heavy chemical inputs.
g12-geography-ug6-t5.summary: Indigenous knowledge is local, orally transmitted, experience-tested community knowledge - the 'people's science' - applied to landscapes, water, soil, pests, agriculture and breeding. In Ethiopia it appears as Maccaa Oromo folk medicine protected in habitats and gardens, Konso dry stone terraces reaching 5 metres with hilltop Paleta towns, Gedeo seera guarding Dhadacha songo trees and agroforestry, and Gumuz faith in Yamba and the Missa, holding resources as communal ancestral heritage under shifting cultivation. Where recorded scientific data is thin, these location-bound practices supplement or substitute for scientific management.

config.title: The Gumuz Chain of Resource Stewardship

steps.label: Gift of Yamba
steps.detail: Natural resources exist as the sacred gift and blessing of Yamba, the supreme deity.

steps.label: Guided by Missa
steps.detail: Each resource has its Missa poly-spirits that ensure proper use and punish violations.

steps.label: Community ownership
steps.detail: Ownership is vested in the whole community; no single member may control it.

steps.label: Fruits only
steps.detail: The present generation holds trusteeship and may use only the fruits of the resources.

steps.label: Pass it on
steps.detail: Knowledge of proper use and the resources themselves pass to the next generation.

config.title: Qualities and Uses of Indigenous Knowledge

questions.q: Indigenous knowledge transmitted orally or by imitation is best described as:
options: Local, orally-transmitted knowledge rooted in everyday experience
questions.explanation: It is rooted in a particular place, transmitted orally or through imitation and demonstration, and reinforced by everyday experience.

questions.q: Indigenous knowledge is frequently referred to as 'people's science' because it is shared to a much greater degree than other forms of knowledge.
questions.explanation: The textbook names it 'people's science' for its highly shared character.

questions.q: The dry stone walled hilltop towns of the Konso are called:
questions.explanation: The Paleta are located on high hills and circled by between one and six rounds of dry stone defensive walls.

questions.q: What is the functional purpose of the Konso terraces?
options: Retain soil from erosion, collect maximum water and discharge the excess
questions.explanation: The terraces retain soil, collect maximum water and discharge the excess, and create terrace saddles used for agriculture.

questions.q: Name the Gedeo sacred ritualistic trees, known as Dhadacha, protected by taboos and traditional rules.
questions.explanation: Songo sacred trees are maintained and protected by prohibition systems (taboos) and traditional seera rules.

questions.q: The Gumuz consider natural resources a private possession of the person who finds them.
questions.explanation: Ownership is vested in the whole community; the present generation runs a trusteeship, and only the fruits may be taken.

questions.q: Who is Yamba in the Gumuz belief system, and what do the Missa do?
questions.answer: Yamba is the supreme deity and Missa are the poly-spirits that ensure proper use|supreme deity|poly-spirits
questions.explanation: Yamba is the gumuz supreme deity, source of life; each resource has its respective Missa (poly-spirits) enforcing proper use, with severe punishments for violations.

questions.q: Which of the following environmental concerns may NOT be solved using indigenous knowledge?
questions.explanation: Indigenous knowledge is applied to ecosystems, water, soil, pests and agriculture - not to modern industrial emission control.

questions.q: State how indigenous knowledge is positioned relative to scientific methods of ecological management.
questions.answer: supplement to scientific methods|substitute for baseline data|supplements or substitutes baseline data
questions.explanation: It is used as a supplement to scientific management and as a substitute for baseline environmental data where little recorded data exists.

questions.q: Arrange the Gumuz chain of stewardship in the correct order.
options: Only the fruits may be taken
Missa ensure proper use and punish violations
Resources pass to the next generation
questions.explanation: Order: Yamba gives the resources, Missa enforce their proper use, the community holds trusteeship, only fruits are taken, and the heritage passes on.

questions.q: Among the Illuababora Maccaa Oromo, deliberately cutting trees and killing animals is seen as breaking the norms and values of society.
questions.explanation: In their belief system, intentional tree cutting and animal killing violate cultural norms, and medicines remain available only as long as the environment is protected.
